title: Carmen

facts.text: Today’s matinee is the Met’s 1,033rd Carmen. The first, on 9 January 1884, drew mixed reviews.
evidence: Carmen (1033)
On 9 January 1884, Carmen was given its first New York Metropolitan Opera performance, to a mixed critical reception.

facts.text: The prelude braids three themes: the bullfighters’ entry, the Toreador refrain, and the motif of Carmen and her fate.
evidence: The prelude to act 1 combines three recurrent themes: the entry of the bullfighters from act 4, the refrain from the Toreador Song from act 2, and the motif that, in two slightly differing forms, represents both Carmen herself and the fate she personifies.

facts.text: Director Carrie Cracknell (Netflix’s Persuasion) made her Met debut with this staging, at the 2023 New Year’s Eve gala.
evidence: New Production, New Year’s Eve Gala
Production Carrie Cracknell [Debut]
Her first feature film, Persuasion, is on Netflix.

facts.text: Micaëla today: Angel Blue. Met debut in 2017, as Mimì; later a Grammy for the Met’s Porgy and Bess.
evidence: She made her Metropolitan Opera début in 2017 as Mimì in La bohème.
She won the Grammy Award for Best Opera Recording for the Metropolitan Opera production of Porgy and Bess

facts.text: Kids’ chorus on the march: conductor Daniele Rustioni sang in La Scala’s boys choir as a child.
evidence: He sang in the boys choir of the Teatro alla Scala in his youth.
Conductor Daniele Rustioni

facts.text: Bizet never visited Spain. For Spanish flavor, he went looking for authentic ethnic material.
evidence: Bizet, who had never visited Spain, sought out appropriate ethnic material to provide an authentic Spanish flavour to his music.

facts.text: Hear that brief phrase? The fate motif announces Carmen’s entrance.
evidence: a brief phrase from the fate motif announces Carmen's entrance

facts.text: Bizet thought the Habanera tune was a folk song. It was by Sebastián Iradier; Bizet credited him in the score.
evidence: adapted from the habanera "El Arreglito ou la Promesse de mariage", by the Spanish musician Sebastián Iradier
which Bizet believed to be a folk song
he added a note about its derivation in the first edition of the vocal score

facts.text: Under the Habanera: a pedal D held throughout, triplets in the voice, and the flute in its low register.
evidence: addition of triplets in the vocal line and the flute in its low register add to the effect
the implied pedal point D is maintained throughout

facts.text: Aigul Akhmetshina, born in Bashkortostan in 1996, also sang Carmen on this staging’s opening night.
evidence: Akhmetshina was born in 1996 in the village of Kirgiz-Miyaki in the Republic of Bashkortostan

facts.text: Piotr Beczała, our Don José, made his Met debut on 19 December 2006, as the Duke in Rigoletto.
evidence: the role in which he also made his Metropolitan Opera, New York, debut on 19 December 2006
Duke in Rigoletto

facts.text: The Seguidilla borrows flamenco rhythms and instruments, and drives José to an exasperated high A-sharp shout.
evidence: notably the "Seguidilla", utilise the rhythms and instrumentation associated with flamenco music
After her beguiling "Seguidilla" provokes José to an exasperated high A sharp shout

facts.text: Before Carmen escapes, a disconcerting fragment of the Habanera returns. Bizet revised this finale several times.
evidence: Carmen's escape is preceded by the brief but disconcerting reprise of a fragment from the habanera
Bizet revised this finale several times to increase its dramatic effect.

facts.text: This entr’acte is built on the melody José will soon sing offstage, on his way back to Carmen.
evidence: Act 2 begins with a short prelude, based on a melody that José will sing offstage before his next entry.

facts.text: Escamillo’s entrance: brass and percussion up front, with the crowd singing along.
evidence: Escamillo's tumultuous entrance, in which brass and percussion provide prominent backing while the crowd sings along

facts.sceneMatch: ^Act\ II:\ Nous\ avons\ en\ tête\ une\ affaire$
facts.text: Kyle Ketelsen, our Escamillo, joined the Army National Guard planning to fly helicopters. Iowa’s music faculty changed that.
evidence: With the intention of becoming a helicopter pilot, he joined the Army National Guard
In 1991 he transferred to the University of Iowa
they encouraged him to become a music major

facts.text: Carmen dances with castanets while a distant cornet calls José to duty, blended into her melody, barely audible.
evidence: Carmen sings, dances and plays the castanets; a distant cornet-call summoning José to duty is blended with Carmen's melody so as to be barely discernible.

facts.text: A muted fate motif on English horn leads in. The Flower Song ends pianissimo, on a sustained high B-flat.
evidence: A muted reference to the fate motif on an English horn leads to José's "Flower Song", a flowing continuous melody that ends pianissimo on a sustained high B-flat.

facts.text: José is swept into the smugglers’ life, and the act closes on a triumphant hymn to freedom.
evidence: José's unavoidable ensnarement into the lawless life culminates musically in the triumphant hymn to freedom that closes the act

facts.text: This entr’acte was first meant for Bizet’s L’Arlésienne. Listen to the woodwinds dialogue and intertwine.
evidence: The prelude to act 3 was originally intended for Bizet's L'Arlésienne score.
with much dialoguing and intertwining between the woodwind instruments

facts.text: The card trio turns ominous when Carmen joins in: the fate motif underlines her premonition of death.
evidence: In the card scene, the lively duet for Frasquita and Mercédès turns ominous when Carmen intervenes; the fate motif underlines her premonition of death.

facts.text: Micaëla’s aria is framed by horn calls, before and after: listen for them.
evidence: Micaëla's aria, after her entry in search of José, is a conventional piece, though of deep feeling, preceded and concluded by horn calls.

facts.text: As Escamillo leaves, his offstage Toreador refrain sounds confident against José’s growing desperation.
evidence: The confident, off-stage sound of the departing Escamillo singing the toreador's refrain provides a distinct contrast to José's increasing desperation.

facts.text: Act IV’s lively entr’acte comes from El criado fingido, a short operetta by Manuel García.
evidence: The final act is prefaced with a lively orchestral piece derived from Manuel García's short operetta El criado fingido.

facts.text: Here come the bullfighters: their march is led by the children’s chorus.
evidence: the bullfighters' march is led by the children's chorus

facts.text: As José kills Carmen, the Toreador refrain rings offstage and the fate motif sounds fortissimo.
evidence: As José kills Carmen, the chorus sing the refrain of the Toreador Song off-stage; the fate motif
is heard fortissimo
